questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Complement of a Set Given Using Ellipsis Notation
questions.problem: If $U={5,10,15,…,50}$ is the universal set and $C={5,15,25,35,45},$ then the complement of $C$ is
questions.worked_solution:
The complement of $C,$ denoted $\overset{―}{C},$ consists of every element in the universal set $U$ that is not in the set $C.$

The elements of $U$ that are not in $C$ are $10,20,30,40,$ and $50.$

Therefore, the complement of $C$ is

$$
\overset{―}{C}={10,20,30,40,50}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Complement of a Set Given Using Ellipsis Notation

questions.problem:
Which of the following are mathematical statements?

- $P:(-2)\cdot 3$

- $Q:5>3$

- $R:7\in N$
questions.worked_solution:
A mathematical statement is a sentence or mathematical expression that is either true or false.

With that in mind, let's examine the given options:

- $P$ is *not* a statement because it is neither true nor false.

- $Q$ is a statement. This statement is *true* because $5$ is larger than  $3.$

- $R$ is a statement. This statement is *true* because $7$ is a natural number.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$Q$ and $R$ only."

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Area Bounded Above a Curve and Below the X-Axis
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14097922/assets/db81a26f1761db677e083d724f3ccb0a8963b9de528c15048bf66cea4aca6179.png)

A region is bounded by the curve $y=-\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)$ and the $x$-axis between $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ as shown above. Find the area of the region.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡(x){|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =1-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $\sqrt{2}-1.$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Area Bounded Above a Curve and Below the X-Axis

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Cubic Polynomial Given Three Real Roots and a Leading Coefficient
questions.problem: The cubic polynomial $P(x)$ has roots ${x}_{1}=-3,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=5,$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $2.$ Find $P(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since our cubic equation has roots ${x}_{1}=-3,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=5,$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $a=2,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2})(x-{x}_{3}) & =2(x-(-3))(x-0)(x-5) \\  & =2x(x+3)(x-5)\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2x(x+3)(x-5) & =2x({x}^{2}-2x-15) \\  & =2({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-15x) \\  & =2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-30x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-30x.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a Cubic Polynomial Given Three Real Roots and a Leading Coefficient

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components
questions.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{d}\,c & =\frac{c\cdot d}{|\,d\,|} \\  & =\frac{{c}_{x}{d}_{x}+{c}_{y}{d}_{y}+{c}_{z}{d}_{z}}{\sqrt{{d}_{x}^{2}+{d}_{y}^{2}+{d}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+2\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of a Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
To find ${A}^{2},$ we multiply $A$ by itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying a Complex Number With No Real or No Imaginary Part Represented by an Argand Diagram
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14097922/assets/99ceba4bbc59ee68728985c41da9ee46fa0fe3448743ab6dcbdc69c642cb3255.png)

What complex number is represented in the Argand diagram above?
questions.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the point are $(0,0).$

- The real part of this complex number is $x=0,$ and

- the imaginary part is $y=0.$

Therefore, the number depicted is $z=0+0\text{i},$ which can be simplfied to $z=0.$

provenance.kp_title: Identifying a Complex Number With No Real or No Imaginary Part Represented by an Argand Diagram
